transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
A commercial flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia
this morning after one of the pilots apparently stabbed the other pilot and tried to crash
the plane with everyone on board.
NPR's Kat Lonsdorf was at the Tel Aviv airport as passengers from that flight finally arrived.
It was a chaotic scene packed with journalists and waiting family members.
Passengers slowly emerged, dragging suitcases, some crying, some smiling and looking relieved.
Some just looked really tired.
There were also quite a few families.
Dan Zolot was traveling with his wife and two small kids and saw much of the incident
on board while trying to comfort his children.
The pilot was stabbed.
I don't know who stabbed him, but I know that three passengers threw themselves on the
terrorist and captured him.
Israeli officials are calling it an attempted terrorist attack, but many details are still
unknown.
The suspect pilot is in custody and Saudi officials have begun an investigation.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
U.S. forces withdrew from Iraq today, two decades after the U.S. invasion of the country
toppled Saddam Hussein.
Iraq's prime minister said it marked a historic new phase.
NPR's Jane Araff was in Baghdad at a rally of Iran-backed militias who were also celebrating.
This is a day of celebration for many Iraqis in many ways.
This particular one is a gathering of three of the main Iran-backed militias who have
declared victory.
They say that they've driven out U.S. forces.
The U.S., of course, said it wanted to leave, needed to leave.
President Trump has said he wants to end these, what he calls, endless wars.
But starting today, it's only Iraq responsible for its security here without the presence
of U.S. forces.
What that means, though, is for groups like this, is that the challenge now is the Iraqi
government confronting paramilitary factions like these, who say they still won't give
up their weapons.
Jane Araff, NPR News, Baghdad.
Louisiana, Alabama, and Arkansas have filed a lawsuit with the U.S. Supreme Court challenging
abortion shield laws of New York, California, and Massachusetts.
Brooke Thorrington from Ember Station WRKF and Baton Rouge has more.
Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrell says the so-called shield laws that allow other
states to send abortion medication through the mail violate the Constitution of federal
law and prevent states with abortion bans from enforcing their own laws.
We want to be able to enforce our laws within the boundaries of our states, and they have
decided that they don't like our laws.
The three states have also filed legal action in the Western District of Louisiana against
30 individuals and organizations that the suit says advertise, prescribe, and ship certain
drugs into states with strict abortion laws.
For NPR News, I'm Brooke Thorrington and Baton Rouge.
Most U.S. stocks fell today.
This is NPR News from Washington.
The Trump administration says it's considering reducing the scope of a border security project
in Big Bend National Park in Texas, but the government also says it's preparing for court
action against landowners who refuse access for the work.
A pause on construction-related activity in the region ends today.
A new report on the state of Switzerland's glaciers reveals they have now lost more than
20 percent of their volume in just five years.
The report warns that glaciers can't survive under such conditions.
Imogen Folks reports.
The latest figures from Switzerland's National Glacier Monitoring Service show the country's
glaciers lost more than 5 percent of their volume this year.
An exceptionally hot summer, with repeated heatwaves, took its toll.
The thawing ice eased Europe's drought somewhat.
But when that ice is gone, water for crops and crucial river transport links like the
Rhine and the Danube will be threatened.
Scientists say the link with global warming is clear.
If temperatures continue to rise, Europe's glaciers may not survive this century.
So far, over a thousand Swiss glaciers have already disappeared.
For NPR News, I'm Imogen Folks in Bairn.
A bear named Backpack has emerged victorious as Fat Bear Week Champion, the heftiest bear
of Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve.
The week of competition celebrates the resilience of the 2,200 brown bears that live in the
preserve on the Alaska Peninsula, which extends from the state's southwest corner to the
Aleutian Islands.

Louisiana, Alabama, and Arkansas file lawsuit challenging abortion shield laws of New York, California, Massachusetts
Trump administration considering reducing scope of border security project in Big Bend National Park Texas
Switzerland's glaciers lose over 20 percent of volume in five years due to climate change
